claim: FPA was first identified as a factor required for the control of Arabidopsis flowering time (Koornneef et al., 1991).
source: The RNA-binding protein FPA was first identified as a factor required for the control of Arabidopsis flowering time (Koornneef et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koornneef et al., 1991.

claim: Loss-of-function fpa mutants flower late due to elevated levels of the floral repressor, FLC (Schomburg et al., 2001).
source: Loss-of-function fpa mutants flower late due to elevated levels of the floral repressor, FLC (Schomburg et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schomburg et al., 2001.

claim: FPA is much more widely conserved than FLC.
source: However, this cannot be the only function of FPA because it is much more widely conserved than FLC.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative knowledge of the conservation of FPA and FLC.

claim: FPA is a member of the spen family of proteins, which are defined by three N-terminal RNA recognition motifs and a C-terminal protein interaction SPOC domain (Ariyoshi and Schwabe, 2003).
source: FPA is a member of the spen family of proteins, which are defined by three N-terminal RNA recognition motifs and a C-terminal protein interaction SPOC domain (Ariyoshi and Schwabe, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ariyoshi and Schwabe, 2003.

claim: FPA controls the site of cleavage and polyadenylation in some mRNAs, including autoregulation of FPA pre-mRNA (Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 2013).
source: We previously showed that FPA controls the site of cleavage and polyadenylation in some mRNAs, including autoregulation of FPA pre-mRNA (Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 2013.

claim: FPA can affect poly(A) site choice at genes with intronic heterochromatin, including RPP7 (Deremetz et al., 2019).
source: These findings were extended to show that FPA can affect poly(A) site choice at genes with intronic heterochromatin, including RPP7 (Deremetz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deremetz et al., 2019.

claim: Plant genomes can encode large numbers of NLR genes, which often occur in physical clusters (Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020; Wei et al., 2016).
source: Plant genomes can encode large numbers of NLR genes, which often occur in physical clusters (Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020; Wei et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020; Wei et al., 2016.

claim: The near-complete repertoire of Arabidopsis NLR genes was only recently revealed using long-read DNA sequencing of diverse Arabidopsis accessions (Van de Weyer et al., 2019).
source: Consequently, the near-complete repertoire of Arabidopsis NLR genes was only recently revealed using long-read DNA sequencing of diverse Arabidopsis accessions (Van de Weyer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van de Weyer et al., 2019.

claim: NLRs can recognise pathogen effectors either directly by binding to them through LRR domains or indirectly by detecting modifications to host proteins caused by effector action.
source: NLRs can recognise pathogen effectors either directly by binding to them through LRR domains or indirectly by detecting modifications to host proteins caused by effector action.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of NLR function.

claim: In some cases, domains of host proteins targeted by pathogen effectors have been incorporated into NLRs as integrated domains (or decoys) (Le Roux et al., 2015).
source: In some cases, domains of host proteins targeted by pathogen effectors have been incorporated into NLRs as integrated domains (or decoys) (Le Roux et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Le Roux et al., 2015.

claim: NLRs that interact directly with effectors are under high levels of diversifying selection to modify their recognition specificities, resulting in significant allelic polymorphism (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).
source: NLRs that interact directly with effectors are under high levels of diversifying selection to modify their recognition specificities, resulting in significant allelic polymorphism (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021.

claim: NLR isoforms that lack NB-ARC or LRR domains can function in plant immune responses (Nishimura et al., 2015; Swiderski et al., 2009; Zhang and Gassmann, 2007).
source: Genomic variation also yields diversity in NLR protein organisation, through domain swapping or truncating mutations, and NLR isoforms that lack NB-ARC or LRR domains can function in plant immune responses (Nishimura et al., 2015; Swiderski et al., 2009; Zhang and Gassmann, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nishimura et al., 2015; Swiderski et al., 2009; Zhang and Gassmann, 2007.

claim: The costs of increased NLR diversity or activity can include detrimental autoimmunity (Rodriguez et al., 2016), reduced association with beneficial microbes (Yang et al., 2010) and a general reduction in fitness (Tian et al., 2003).
source: The benefit of NLRs to the host is disease resistance, but the costs of increased NLR diversity or activity can include detrimental autoimmunity (Rodriguez et al., 2016), reduced association with beneficial microbes (Yang et al., 2010) and a general reduction in fitness (Tian et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rodriguez et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2003.

claim: Autoimmunity caused by epistatic interactions involving NLRs can cause hybrid necrosis (Chae et al., 2014).
source: In some cases, autoimmunity caused by epistatic interactions involving NLRs can cause hybrid necrosis (Chae et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chae et al., 2014.

claim: MicroRNAs limit the expression of many NLRs by targeting conserved regions encoded in NLR mRNAs and triggering cascades of phased siRNAs that broadly suppress NLR activity (Cai et al., 2018; Canto-Pastor et al., 2019; Shivaprasad et al., 2012; Zhai et al., 2011).
source: For example, microRNAs limit the expression of many NLRs by targeting conserved regions encoded in NLR mRNAs and triggering cascades of phased siRNAs that broadly suppress NLR activity (Cai et al., 2018; Canto-Pastor et al., 2019; Shivaprasad et al., 2012; Zhai et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2018; Canto-Pastor et al., 2019; Shivaprasad et al., 2012; Zhai et al., 2011.

claim: Alternative splicing is required for the functions of both the N gene which provides resistance to tobacco mosaic virus (Dinesh-Kumar and Baker, 2000), and RECOGNITION OF PSEUDOMONAS SYRINGAE 4 (RPS4), which confers resistance to Pseudomonas syringae DC3000 in Arabidopsis (Zhang and Gassmann, 2007).
source: Alternative splicing, which promotes the simultaneous expression of more than one NLR isoform, is required for the functions of both the N gene which provides resistance to tobacco mosaic virus (Dinesh-Kumar and Baker, 2000), and RECOGNITION OF PSEUDOMONAS SYRINGAE 4 (RPS4), which confers resistance to Pseudomonas syringae DC3000 in Arabidopsis (Zhang and Gassmann, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dinesh-Kumar and Baker, 2000; Zhang and Gassmann, 2007.

claim: Alternative polyadenylation at intragenic heterochromatin controls the expression of Arabidopsis RECOGNITION OF PERONOSPORA PARASITICA 7 (RPP7), with functional consequences for immunity against the oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (Tsuchiya and Eulgem, 2013).
source: Alternative polyadenylation at intragenic heterochromatin controls the expression of Arabidopsis RECOGNITION OF PERONOSPORA PARASITICA 7 (RPP7), with functional consequences for immunity against the oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (Tsuchiya and Eulgem, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsuchiya and Eulgem, 2013.

claim: Null mutants defective in nonsense-mediated RNA decay (NMD) are lethal in Arabidopsis because they trigger NLR RPS6-dependent autoimmunity (Gloggnitzer et al., 2014).
source: For example, null mutants defective in nonsense-mediated RNA decay (NMD) are lethal in Arabidopsis because they trigger NLR RPS6-dependent autoimmunity (Gloggnitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gloggnitzer et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations in the RNA exosome, which degrades RNAs in a 3′ to 5′ direction, suppress RPS6-dependent autoimmune phenotypes (Takagi et al., 2020).
source: Conversely, mutations in the RNA exosome, which degrades RNAs in a 3′ to 5′ direction, suppress RPS6-dependent autoimmune phenotypes (Takagi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takagi et al., 2020.

claim: Using in vivo interaction proteomics–mass spectrometry (IVI-MS), 203 FPA co-purifying proteins with a median log2 fold change in abundance of greater than two were identified.
source: By comparing the proteins detected in three biological replicates of 35S::FPA:YFP and Col-0, we identified 203 FPA co-purifying proteins with a median log2 fold change in adundance of greater than two (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from IVI-MS experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: At least 56% (113) of the enriched proteins are poly(A)+mRNA binding proteins as established by orthogonal RNA-binding proteome analysis (Bach-Pages et al., 2020; Reichel et al., 2016).
source: At least 56% (113) of the enriched proteins are poly(A)+mRNA binding proteins as established by orthogonal RNA-binding proteome analysis (Bach-Pages et al., 2020; Reichel et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bach-Pages et al., 2020; Reichel et al., 2016.

claim: 14 highly conserved cleavage and polyadenylation factors (CPFs) co-purified with FPA.
source: Consistent with FPA control of mRNA 3′ end formation, 14 highly conserved cleavage and polyadenylation factors (CPFs) co-purified with FPA (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The U2AF and U2 spliceosome components that interact with CFIm–CPSF to mediate terminal exon definition were detected (Kyburz et al., 2006; Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
source: The U2AF and U2 spliceosome components that interact with CFIm–CPSF to mediate terminal exon definition were also detected (Kyburz et al., 2006; Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kyburz et al., 2006 and data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Both subunits of Pol II were detected in the FPA co-purification.
source: We additionally detected both subunits of Pol II.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from IVI-MS experiments.

claim: The kinase CDKC;2, which phosphorylates Ser2 (Wang et al., 2014), and the phosphatase CPL1 (homolog of yeast Fcp1), which dephosphorylates Ser5 (Koiwa et al., 2004), co-purified with FPA.
source: We found that the kinase CDKC;2, which phosphorylates Ser2 (Wang et al., 2014), and the phosphatase CPL1 (homolog of yeast Fcp1), which dephosphorylates Ser5 (Koiwa et al., 2004), co-purified with FPA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from IVI-MS experiments and citations to Wang et al., 2014; Koiwa et al., 2004.

claim: The homolog of the human exonuclease XRN2 (known as XRN3 in Arabidopsis), which mediates Pol II transcription termination (Krzyszton et al., 2018), was detected.
source: We also detected the homolog of the human exonuclease XRN2 (known as XRN3 in Arabidopsis), which mediates Pol II transcription termination (Krzyszton et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from IVI-MS experiments and a citation to Krzyszton et al., 2018.

claim: FPA is enriched at the 3′ end of genes and co-localises with Pol II phosphorylated at Ser2 of the CTD.
source: Our metagene analysis revealed that FPA is enriched at the 3′ end of genes and co-localises with Pol II phosphorylated at Ser2 of the CTD (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: FPA occupancy at 3' ends was well correlated with Pol II Ser2 occupancy (Spearman's ρ = 0.67, p<2 × 10−308, 95% confidence interval [0.66, 0.68]).
source: We found that FPA occupancy at 3' ends was well correlated with Pol II Ser2 occupancy (Spearman's ρ = 0.67, p<2 × 10−308, 95% confidence interval [0.66, 0.68]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: FPA is required for 3′ end processing at PIF5 (Duc et al., 2013).
source: For example, we previously showed that FPA is required for 3′ end processing at PIF5 (Duc et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duc et al., 2013.

claim: Pol II Ser2 was enriched at the 3′ end of PIF5 in Col-0 but depleted from this region in fpa-7 mutants.
source: Pol II Ser2 was enriched at the 3′ end of PIF5 in Col-0 but depleted from this region in fpa-7 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: FPA autoregulates its expression by promoting premature cleavage and polyadenylation within intron 1 of FPA pre-mRNA (Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010).
source: FPA autoregulates its expression by promoting premature cleavage and polyadenylation within intron 1 of FPA pre-mRNA (Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duc et al., 2013; Hornyik et al., 2010.

claim: A proximal poly(A) site in the first intron and distal sites in the terminal intron and exon of FPA could be mapped in Col-0 using Nanopore and Helicos DRS.
source: Consistent with this, a proximal poly(A) site in the first intron and distal sites in the terminal intron and exon of FPA could be mapped in Col-0 using Nanopore and Helicos DRS (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A quantitative shift towards selection of distal poly(A) sites in the loss-of-function fpa-8 mutant and a strong shift to proximal poly(A) site selection when FPA is overexpressed was detected using all three data types.
source: Using all three data types, we detected a quantitative shift towards selection of distal poly(A) sites in the loss-of-function fpa-8 mutant and a strong shift to proximal poly(A) site selection when FPA is overexpressed (35S::FPA:YFP).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Illumina RNA-Seq, Helicos DRS, and Nanopore DRS.

claim: Using Nanopore DRS, 285 and 293 loci with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively, were identified.
source: Using this approach on Nanopore DRS data, we identified 285 and 293 loci with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 77.9% (222) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in fpa-8 displayed a positive change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a predominant shift to distal poly(A) site selection.
source: In all, 77.9% (222) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in fpa-8 displayed a positive change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a predominant shift to distal poly(A) site selection (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 56.7% (166) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP displayed a negative change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a shift towards proximal poly(A) sites.
source: In contrast, 56.7% (166) of loci with alternative polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP displayed a negative change in the mean 3′ end position, indicating a shift towards proximal poly(A) sites (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 16 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) site selection in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) site selection in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=3.9 × 10−7).
source: A total of 16 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) site selection in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) site selection in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=3.9 × 10−7), demonstrating that loss of function versus overexpression of FPA can result in reciprocal patterns of poly(A) site choice.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Nanopore DRS data.

claim: Using Helicos DRS, 319 and 299 genes with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively, were identified.
source: We used the same approach to identify loci with FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation in Helicos DRS data. We identified 319 and 299 genes with alternative polyadenylation events in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP, respectively (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The predominant shifts in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP were towards distal (79.0% or 252 loci) and proximal (75.3% or 225 loci) poly(A) sites, respectively, as detected by Helicos DRS.
source: Consistent with Nanopore DRS analysis, the predominant shifts in fpa-8 and 35S::FPA:YFP were towards distal (79.0% or 252 loci) and proximal (75.3% or 225 loci) poly(A) sites, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis.

claim: 44 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) sites in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=4.8 × 10−30) as detected by Helicos DRS.
source: In all, 44 loci displayed a shift to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 and to proximal poly(A) sites in 35S::FPA:YFP (hypergeometric test p=4.8 × 10−30), again demonstrating reciprocal poly(A) site selection depending on FPA activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Helicos DRS data.

claim: Of the 222 loci identified with shifts to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 using Nanopore DRS, 39.6% (88) were also detected using Helicos DRS.
source: Of the 222 loci identified with shifts to distal poly(A) sites in fpa-8 using Nanopore DRS, 39.6% (88) were also detected using Helicos DRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Nanopore and Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 44.0% of loci (73) with proximal polyadenylation detected in 35S::FPA:YFP using Nanopore DRS were also detected using Helicos DRS.
source: Likewise, 44.0% of loci (73) with proximal polyadenylation detected in 35S::FPA:YFP using Nanopore DRS were also detected using Helicos DRS.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Nanopore and Helicos DRS data.

claim: Using Illumina RNA-Seq, 2535 loci with differential RNA processing events in fpa-8 were identified: 1792 were upregulated, 390 were downregulated, and 353 had both upregulated and downregulated regions (FDR < 0.05, absolute logFC >1).
source: Using this approach, we identified 2535 loci with differential RNA processing events in fpa-8: 1792 were upregulated, 390 were downregulated, and 353 had both upregulated and downregulated regions (FDR < 0.05, absolute logFC >1; Figure 2F, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: 1747 loci with differential RNA processing events were identified in 35S::FPA:YFP: 997 were upregulated, 532 were downregulated, and 218 had both upregulated and downregulated regions.
source: A total of 1747 loci with differential RNA processing events were identified in 35S::FPA:YFP: 997 were upregulated, 532 were downregulated, and 218 had both upregulated and downregulated regions (Figure 2F, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by Illumina RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FPA does not influence global levels of mRNA m6A methylation.
source: However, we detected no differences in the m6A level between genotypes with altered FPA activity. Therefore, we conclude that FPA does not influence global levels of mRNA m6A methylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis of m6A/A ratios.

claim: Only 10.6% of loci with altered poly(A) site choice in 35S::FPA:YFP have altered H3K9me2 in ibm1 mutants compared with 14.2% of all loci tested (hypergeometric p=0.97).
source: When we analysed two independent ChIP-Seq datasets of H3K9me2 in ibm1–4 mutants (Inagaki et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2020), we found that only 10.6% of loci with altered poly(A) site choice in 35S::FPA:YFP have altered H3K9me2 in ibm1 mutants compared with 14.2% of all loci tested (hypergeometric p=0.97; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ChIP-Seq data from Inagaki et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2020, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: FPA-dependent poly(A) site choice is not an indirect consequence of FPA control of IBM1.
source: This result suggests that FPA-dependent poly(A) site choice is not an indirect consequence of FPA control of IBM1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis of H3K9me2 ChIP-Seq data in ibm1 mutants.

claim: Sequences encoding NB-ARC, Rx-like coiled coil (CC), and/or LRR domains were enriched amongst the loci with increased proximal polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP.
source: We found that sequences encoding NB-ARC, Rx-like coiled coil (CC), and/or LRR domains were enriched amongst the loci with increased proximal polyadenylation in 35S::FPA:YFP (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The TNL gene AT5G46490, located in the RPS6 cluster, is incorrectly annotated as two loci, AT5G46490 and AT5G46500.
source: For example, we found that the TNL gene AT5G46490, located in the RPS6 cluster, is incorrectly annotated as two loci, AT5G46490 and AT5G46500 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: AT5G46490 is actually a single locus with a previously unrecognised 2.7 kb intron containing a proximal poly(A) site, the use of which is controlled by FPA.
source: Nanopore DRS evidence indicates that this is actually a single locus with a previously unrecognised 2.7 kb intron containing a proximal poly(A) site, the use of which is controlled by FPA.
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data.

claim: The 3′UTR of RPS6 is complex, with multiple splicing events and poly(A) sites.
source: Nanopore DRS indicates that the 3′UTR of RPS6 is complex, with multiple splicing events and poly(A) sites (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: An independent unannotated gene that overlaps the RPS6 3′UTR was detected.
source: We also detected transcripts expressed from this region that do not appear to be contiguous with RPS6 3′UTR reads. Instead, these reads correspond to an independent unannotated gene that overlaps the RPS6 3′UTR.
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data.

claim: The unannotated gene overlapping RPS6 3′UTR encodes a TIR domain similar to that of RPS6.
source: The gene encodes a TIR domain similar to that of RPS6 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein alignment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Of the 206 NLR genes examined, 124 had a sufficient level of expression to identify alternative polyadenylation in the Nanopore DRS data.
source: Of the 206 NLR genes examined, 124 had a sufficient level of expression to identify alternative polyadenylation in the Nanopore DRS data; of these 124, 62 (50.0%) were found to have FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation (Tables 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claim: Of the 124 expressed NLRs, 62 (50.0%) were found to have FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation.
source: Of the 206 NLR genes examined, 124 had a sufficient level of expression to identify alternative polyadenylation in the Nanopore DRS data; of these 124, 62 (50.0%) were found to have FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation (Tables 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claim: Of the 74 expressed NLRs located in major clusters, 44 (59.5%) were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02).
source: Of the 74 expressed NLRs located in major clusters, 44 (59.5%) were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02) (Lee and Chae, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Nanopore DRS data and a citation to Lee and Chae, 2020.

claim: 20 (71.4%) of the 28 expressed NLRs reported to be under high levels of diversifying selection were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02).
source: Consistent with this, 20 (71.4%) of the 28 expressed NLRs reported to be under high levels of diversifying selection were sensitive to FPA activity (chi2p=0.02) (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of Nanopore DRS data and a citation to Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021.

claim: FPA-sensitive NLRs tended to be located in regions with higher levels of synteny diversity, although the association was not significant (t-test p=0.09).
source: In addition, FPA-sensitive NLRs tended to be located in regions with higher levels of synteny diversity (Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020), although in this case the association was not significant (t-test p=0.09; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of synteny diversity data from Jiao and Schneeberger, 2020, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation is associated with rapidly evolving NLRs.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that FPA-dependent alternative polyadenylation is associated with rapidly evolving NLRs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the association of FPA-sensitive NLRs with major clusters, high diversifying selection, and synteny diversity.

claim: For 17 NLR genes, a change in FPA activity altered the formation of readthrough or chimeric RNAs containing one or more NLR loci.
source: For 17 NLR genes, we found that a change in FPA activity altered the formation of readthrough or chimeric RNAs containing one or more NLR loci (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claim: The duplicated RPP7a/b-like genes AT1G58848 and AT1G59218 displayed increased readthrough into downstream transposable elements (TEs) in fpa-8.
source: The duplicated RPP7a/b-like genes AT1G58848 and AT1G59218 (which form part of the RPP7 cluster containing five CNL-class NLRs) displayed increased readthrough into downstream transposable elements (TEs) in fpa-8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The TNL-class gene AT1G63730, located in the B4/RLM1 cluster, forms chimeric RNA with the downstream TNL-class gene AT1G63740 in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 1099, FDR = 0.02).
source: For example, the TNL-class gene AT1G63730, located in the B4/RLM1 cluster, forms chimeric RNA with the downstream TNL-class gene AT1G63740 in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 1099, FDR = 0.02; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 17 NLR genes with intronic polyadenylation controlled by FPA were identified.
source: We identified another 17 NLR genes with intronic polyadenylation controlled by FPA (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claim: A proximal poly(A) site within the third intron of AT1G69550 results in mRNAs with a premature stop codon; the encoded protein lacks most of the predicted LRR domain.
source: For example, we identified a proximal poly(A) site within the third intron of AT1G69550, which encodes a TNL-type singleton NLR (Figure 4B). Use of this poly(A) site results in mRNAs with a premature stop codon; the encoded protein lacks most of the predicted LRR domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In fpa-8, readthrough at the proximal poly(A) site in AT1G69550 is increased (Helicos EMD = 1271, FDR = 1.2 × 10−4), resulting in an increase in the relative number of full-length transcripts.
source: In fpa-8, readthrough at this poly(A) site is increased (Helicos EMD = 1271, FDR = 1.2 × 10−4), resulting in an increase in the relative number of full-length transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis.

claim: 45 NLRs were controlled by premature termination within exons.
source: The most common form of FPA-dependent NLR regulation was premature termination within exons (Table 3). We identified 45 NLRs controlled in this way: at 44 of these loci, termination occurred within protein-coding exons.
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data analysis.

claim: At RPP28 (AT2G14080), multiple exonic poly(A) sites located within the second and fourth exons were detected.
source: For example, at RPP28 (AT2G14080), which encodes a TNL-class singleton NLR, we detected multiple exonic poly(A) sites located within the second and fourth exons, which encode the NB-ARC and LRR domains, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanopore DRS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Selection of exonic poly(A) sites at RPP28 was increased in 35S::FPA:YFP (Helicos EMD = 859, FDR = 5.4 × 10−9) and decreased in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 912, FDR = 7.6 × 10−9).
source: Selection of these exonic poly(A) sites was increased in 35S::FPA:YFP (Helicos EMD = 859, FDR = 5.4 × 10−9) and decreased in fpa-8 (Helicos EMD = 912, FDR = 7.6 × 10−9).
evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data analysis.

claim: At RPP13 (AT3G46530), FPA overexpression causes selection of proximal poly(A) sites located within the region encoding the LRR domain (Helicos EMD = 228, FDR = 1.8 × 10−4).
source: For example, at RPP13 (AT3G46530), which encodes a CNL-class NLR protein, FPA overexpression causes selection of proximal poly(A) sites located within the region encoding the LRR domain (Helicos EMD = 228, FDR = 1.8 × 10−4; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Helicos DRS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: At AT5G40060, FPA-dependent proximal polyadenylation in the region encoding the NB-ARC domain results in a transcript containing only the uORF, which is not a predicted NMD target and may be more efficiently translated into a TIR-only protein.
